Cet article est né de la réponse de Slim: This article grew out of a response by Slim Hammami, program coordinator at the Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel de Montréal-Nord, to an opinion letter by Patrick Lavallée, former commander of PDQ 39, published in Le Journal de Montréal. By challenging, among other things, the use of the expression “lawless zone,” Mr. Hammami opened up a broader reflection on how Montréal-Nord is described and on the effects these portrayals can have on its residents.
Le sujet a ensuite évolué au fil de notr: The subject then evolved over the course of our fieldwork. At Le Carignan park and at the Place Bourassa shopping centre, the accounts we gathered from residents revealed a gap between certain portrayals of the neighbourhood and the daily experience of those who live there.
Nous avons ensuite soumis cette réflexio: We then put this reflection to Michel Parazelli, associate professor at UQAM’s School of Social Work, to better understand the concept of “territorial stigma,” its mechanisms and its effects.
Enfin, au cours de la préparation de l’a: Finally, while preparing the article, we discovered how the borough of Montréal-Nord is trying to push back against labels and take control of the narrative that describes the neighbourhood.
Le sujet s’est ainsi élargi : d’une cont: The subject thus grew wider: from a controversy over a few words used to describe one area of Montréal-Nord, it became a reflection on who tells the story of a territory, which portrayals take hold, and how the people who live there are trying to take back their own story.
<strong>À Montréal-Nord, les habitants e: In Montréal-Nord, residents and organizations have long contested the labels that associate their neighbourhood with violence, crime and poverty. The borough itself has launched the “Mille histoires, une communauté” initiative to take back control of its image. As the PDQ 39 scandal reignites tensions around policing, one question remains: who tells the story of Montréal-Nord? And what effects does that story have on the people who live there?
En cette journée d’août, le parc Le Cari: On this August day, Le Carignan park in Montréal-Nord looks nothing like the images its name is often associated with. On the basketball courts, players fight for every ball while spectators packed around the sidelines cheer on the teams. A few metres away, children cool off in the water games under their parents’ watchful eyes. It is the 32<sup>nd</sup> edition of the Tournoi de Basket de Rue, which over the years has become an important gathering for Montréal-Nord’s youth and community. The event has seen the likes of players who went on to the NBA, including Chris Boucher, Luguentz Dort and Bennedict Mathurin.
À une vingtaine de mètres des terrains,: About twenty metres from the courts, sitting in the grass, Ahmad Mathi watches the young people play. He has lived in Montréal-Nord since 2022 with his wife and their three children. His experience of the neighbourhood differs from the one people around him sometimes reflect back to him. He is regularly asked why he chose to live in a “dangerous corner” with “lots of crime” and gangs. Yet, he tells La Converse, “To this day, I’ve never witnessed a scene of violence. No one has ever attacked me.” For him, the risk depends more on who you hang out with than on where you live.
La scène ordinaire (un tournoi, des fami: This ordinary scene (a tournament, families, children playing, neighbours catching up) doesn’t mean Montréal-Nord is spared social hardship or episodes of violence. Rather, it is a reminder that a territory is not reduced to the incidents that make headlines.
C’est précisément cette distance entre c: It is precisely this distance between what is lived in the neighbourhood and what is said about it that lies at the heart of a new controversy, one that is shifting the debate sparked by the <l1>scandal at Neighbourhood Station 39</l1>.
Le 25 juin dernier, Patrick Lavallée, in: On June 25, Patrick Lavallée, a retired SPVM inspector and former commander of PDQ 39, published an opinion letter in Le Journal de Montréal. Without downplaying the allegations against certain officers, he defended the work carried out under his leadership from 2019 to 2022 and described a police force that was “present, professional, accountable, competent and rooted in its community.”
Pour illustrer les défis auxquels ses éq: To illustrate the challenges his teams faced, he described the area around the corner of Pascal and Lapierre streets as a “lawless zone” where “criminals acted with complete impunity.” In this regard, he defended a strategy based on sustained police presence, intelligence and collaboration with community organizations.
Le 4 août, le Café-Jeunesse Multiculture: On August 4, the Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel de Montréal-Nord replied in an open letter. Without denying the security issues, its program coordinator, Slim Hammami, argued that certain words used to describe the neighbourhood help reinforce the prejudices that the borough’s residents suffer from.
Le désaccord porte aussi sur la manière: The disagreement is also about how to tell the story of Montréal-Nord. For Patrick Lavallée, the territory is first and foremost what the police must respond to, notably by identifying problems and ensuring safety. For Slim Hammami, this reading risks instead reducing the neighbourhood to its difficulties and sustaining what researchers call “territorial stigma.” The consequences can go beyond the neighbourhood’s image. The Café-Jeunesse points in particular to young people who avoid putting their address on their résumé or mentioning that they live in Montréal-Nord, for fear of being judged before they even have a chance to introduce themselves.
<strong>« Ici, ce n’est pas ce que les m: “Here, it’s not what the words say”
Sur le terrain, le décalage entre l’imag: On the ground, the gap between the image of Montréal-Nord and its residents’ experience quickly becomes apparent. The people we met don’t deny the neighbourhood’s problems. They simply refuse to let those problems be enough to define it.
Ryan, 17 ans, y a toujours vécu. Il reco: Ryan, 17, has always lived here. He acknowledges there are problems, but refuses to see them as unique to Montréal-Nord. “I think people talk badly about [the neighbourhood], when it’s a neighbourhood I think is good. I feel safe inside it,” he says. Problematic behaviour, he adds, “exists everywhere; it’s not specific to Montréal-Nord.”
Hatim, 16 ans, estime pour sa part que l: Hatim, 16, believes that the image of a dangerous neighbourhood belongs more to the past. Since he moved here, he says, he has never been in a situation where he felt in danger. He stresses instead the diversity of Montréal-Nord and the coexistence of its different communities. “Montréal-Nord, personally, I say it, I think it’s one of the best neighbourhoods in Montréal,” he says.
Akram, qui connaît le quartier par son a: Akram, who knows the neighbourhood through his business, also describes a daily life that is “pretty quiet.” He acknowledges that the borough’s bad reputation is stubborn: “It’s true that it used to be a dangerous neighbourhood here. But for a while now, things have calmed down quite a bit, and the reputation won’t change overnight.” For him, the image projected of Montréal-Nord no longer necessarily matches reality: “People will still think it’s a dangerous neighbourhood [...] when that’s not really what’s actually happening.”
Hélène, qui travaille dans un domaine in: Hélène, who works in a field somewhere between community work and administration, adds another nuance. “It’s very hard to talk about Montréal-Nord as a whole,” she says, noting that the borough brings together areas with different social realities. She also points to community and cultural activities and to initiatives aimed at young people: “There’s a lot of effort on the community side to mobilize young people, to get them involved in projects.”
Ces témoignages ne décrivent donc ni un: These accounts therefore describe neither a neighbourhood without problems nor the “ghetto” of certain public discourse. They show a territory shaped by multiple realities: those of social hardship and violence, but also those of work, families, businesses, diversity, solidarity and community life.
Depuis quelque temps, l’arrondissement c: For some time now, the borough has also been seeking to change how Montréal-Nord is perceived. Under the tagline “Mille histoires, une communauté,” it has launched a new visual identity meant to “take back control of its story” and to fight the prejudices that associate the borough with danger, violence, poverty and crime.
La démarche repose notamment sur des ate: The approach relies in particular on workshops bringing together residents, organizations, business people, employees and elected officials of the borough. The stated goal is threefold: to change how Montréal-Nord is viewed from the outside, to put an end to the stigmatization its population faces, and also to nurture the pride and sense of belonging of those who live there.
Dans ses réponses à La Converse, le cabi: In its responses to La Converse, the office of Mayor Christine Black acknowledges that this effort is partly motivated by the image projected by the media. According to the borough, media coverage “focuses more on the bad than on the good” and thus helps sustain a negative perception of the territory, even though, according to the office, Montréal-Nord is experiencing a momentum of revitalization.
L’arrondissement ne présente donc pas ce: The borough therefore does not present this new identity as a mere communications exercise, since it believes a neighbourhood’s image can have concrete consequences for its future: sense of belonging, retention of residents, investment, employment, housing and how much people visit the area.
Cette volonté de reprendre le contrôle d: This desire to take back control of its story directly echoes what some residents and organizations are calling for: to stop letting a few episodes of violence or a few labels define Montréal-Nord.
Le débat suscité par l’ancien commandant: The debate sparked by the former PDQ 39 commander and the Café-Jeunesse is not a simple disagreement over word choice. It points to a concept well known to researchers: “territorial stigma.”
Pour Michel Parazelli, professeur associ: For Michel Parazelli, associate professor at UQAM’s School of Social Work, a place never has a single meaning. “The same place, with its objective characteristics, can have a different meaning for different people,” he explains. As an example, he cites public housing (HLMs), “often connoted as something inferior, with inadequate living conditions. Whereas for the people who live in HLMs, […] it’s flat-out their home, their house, the place where they can recognize a bit of their life story.”
Selon le chercheur, c’est la répétition: According to the researcher, it is the repetition of certain negative labels that ends up reducing a neighbourhood to a single identity. Expressions like “ghetto,” “slum” or “lawless zone” no longer merely describe a situation; they become categories that lock a territory into a lasting representation.
Cette représentation est ensuite aliment: This representation is then fed by various social actors. The media, institutions, political leaders and police services can, sometimes despite themselves, help associate a neighbourhood with a few powerful images, such as crime, poverty and violence, at the expense of its full complexity. For the researcher, negative labels can then function as “communication shortcuts” that simplify far more complex social situations.
Le professeur insiste toutefois sur un p: The professor insists on one point, however: acknowledging the existence of a territorial stigma is not the same as denying the very real difficulties some neighbourhoods face. Rather, he believes the way they are described influences the responses that will then be favoured. In his view, Patrick Lavallée’s text illustrates this tension. Mr. Parazelli acknowledges that, for police officers, “there is a territory here that is threatening, and we are here to defend other people who find it threatening.” But this reading can, in his view, “feed divisions” and push into the shadows “the social, economic and cultural logics” that explain the situations observed.
Pour le chercheur, l’enjeu dépasse donc: For the researcher, the issue therefore goes well beyond the case of Montréal-Nord. The way a society tells the story of its working-class neighbourhoods also shapes how it chooses to intervene in them: through control and correction, or through recognition of lived realities and support for the people who live there.
Montréal-Nord est raconté par ceux qui l: Montréal-Nord is described by those who observe it, administer it or intervene in it: media, police, elected officials, organizations, researchers. Residents, for their part, often speak after the fact, once the neighbourhood’s story is already set.
Cette question était déjà apparue lors d: This question had already come up at the <l1>dialogue evening “How do we counter police brutality?”</l1>, organized by La Converse, the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel, the Coalition Pozé and the Clinique juridique de Saint-Michel. Samuel Bunche, who grew up in the borough and is involved in its community life, summed it up at a dialogue evening organized by La Converse: “If people hear about Montréal-Nord, of course they’re terrified.” Once you’re there, he says, “you discover there’s a lot of good. But it’s good that’s very, very much smothered.”
Lors du<l1> 5</l1><sup><l1>e</l1></sup><: At the <l1>5</l1><sup><l1>th</l1></sup><l1> symposium</l1> “Urbanité et jeunes marginalisés,” organized in Montréal-Nord on April 30 by the Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel, sociologist Saïd Bouamama showed how this stigmatization can end up being attributed to the residents themselves: violence, failure or marginality are associated with the place, while the social realities running through them fade into the background. The address can then become a social marker.
La question devient alors : qui a le pou: The question then becomes: who has the power to select what deserves to be told – the shooting or the park, crime or the families who live there?
<strong>Peut-on changer le récit sans ni: Can the story change without denying the problems?
Le 11 août dernier, cette question a qui: On August 11, this question left the realm of the battle of ideas and landed at the heart of a public meeting at Montréal city hall. For four and a half hours, dozens of citizens questioned Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) chief Fady Dagher about the allegations involving PDQ 39, but also about the racial profiling and police practices they say they have endured for years.
Anastasia Marcellin, qui affirme dénonce: Anastasia Marcellin, who says she has been denouncing racism problems at PDQ 39 since 2009, asked why these alleged behaviours had not been dealt with sooner. “It’s not just Neighbourhood Station 39. The problem isn’t just the officers, it’s the system,” she said.
Le chef du SPVM a reconnu que son organi: The SPVM chief acknowledged that his organization may have “blind spots” and promised a “real culture change.” But he also defended the decision to keep the criminal investigation under the SPVM’s responsibility, arguing that a transfer would risk delaying the process.
Dans la salle, deux conceptions de Montr: In the room, two conceptions of Montréal-Nord were thus once again pitted against each other. That of an institution seeking to correct its practices in response to documented problems, and that of citizens who believe these problems have been known for far too long to be reduced to a few individual behaviours.
Pour Michel Parazelli, cette distinction: For Michel Parazelli, this distinction is essential. “When we stigmatize and point the finger at people who live in places that are not socially accepted, we feed the divide and we push into the shadows […] the social, economic and cultural logics that can account for the existence of these situations.”
La bataille autour de Montréal-Nord ne p: The battle over Montréal-Nord is therefore not only about the words used to describe the neighbourhood, but also about the power to define what deserves to be seen, told and remembered. The borough has chosen to take back this story with the “Mille histoires, une communauté” initiative. Organizations and residents, for their part, have long asked that their reality not be reduced to crime, violence and police interventions.
Une nouvelle identité visuelle ne peut c: A new visual identity cannot, on its own, erase a stigma built up over the years. It can, however, shift the gaze, provided the thousand stories it promises truly find their place in the story of Montréal-Nord.
